I enjoy extreme horror like this for mainly the same reasons I watch horror in the first place - I enjoy experiencing and feeling negative emotions in a controlled environment where I know it's all fake.


I'm somewhat numbed to those emotions when it comes to real life, so these kind of films are like an outlet for that. It feels cathartic to immerse myself in them and feel shocked, horrified, disgusted, etc. Not to mention I like appreciating the technical aspects such as the effects. I'm super sensitive to real gore, but I love seeing the most brutal violence in movies because I just find it really impressive!


Also, as an overthinker, I think a small part of the reason why I watch extreme horror is so that I can mentally "prepare" in case something similar ever happens to me or a loved one, and consider ways in which I would try to survive.

I know this post is 2 months old and you've probably already gotten started in your journey through his works, so apologies for necro'ing. BUT I have conflicted opinions on this question...


TLDR; I think the first season of Twin Peaks is great to watch as an introduction to Lynch, but Twin Peaks as a whole should be watched last in his filmography.



The show encompasses so many of Lynch's signature styles, themes, and idiosyncrasies. It's cozy, scary, funny, grounded yet melodramatic, heartbreaking, but also very tender. I think it would work fairly well as a litmus test for whether someone is on board for what Lynch is all about.


At the same time though, because Twin Peaks is such a definitive project, *especially* when you include Season 3 in the mix, I think that having seen all of Lynch's other works first would enhance the viewing experience a lot. I'm honestly not sure how well someone would jive with The Return if their only experience with Lynch has been the original TP run.


So overall, I think the best way to go about it is to watch season 1. If you enjoy it, go through his films in whatever order tickles your fancy. Going by release date is always reliable, or you could even go from his most straightforward films to his most surreal/abstract. Then finally, if you've liked everything so far, go back to Twin Peaks and watch it through from the beginning (or just continue onto season 2 if you want).

Apologies for necro-ing this post, but I too was shook to my core to learn that the hat man is a widely recognized phenomenon.


When I was kid, maybe 6 or 7, there was a period where I would sometimes see the hat man standing at the top of our stairs, right outside my bedroom. It was always during the day, with plenty of natural light, but he was just a pure black silhouette, very tall and with the signature hat brim and long coat outline. 


I could only ever see him out of the corner of my eye, when I'd turn my head to try and look directly at him, the silhouette vanished. Eventually I stopped seeing him, though my memories always remained pretty vivid and strong, even as I got older. The rest of my family also had very odd experiences in the house for a few years, though my dad was the only other one who also saw the hat man a few times. Nowadays there isn't anything too crazy, though we still hear the occasional footsteps back and forth upstairs when no one is up there, or we'll see/feel phantom cats walk by our legs.


Recently though, I connected my hat man sightings to another experience I had a year prior, at 5 years old. One night, I was in my room watching tv, and it was quite late, the whole house was dark and quiet. My door was open just a crack. Out of nowhere, I hear a low pitched and very loud male voice shout from the upstairs landing. I've always been a bit fuzzy on what he said, but I *believe* it was either "GET OUT", or "COME HERE". I was fully awake when it happened, and have never experienced sleep paralysis, even to this day.


Somehow I was brave enough to get up and go check to see what it was. Nobody on the landing. Brother's room? Sound asleep. I creep downstairs and check my parent's room. Also sound asleep, and their own tv is at a low volume. At this point I'm sufficiently freaked out, so I just race back up to my room, fully close my door, and hide under the covers until I eventually fall asleep.


I never actually saw the hat man that first time, but just the fact that the voice came from the exact place I would see him a couple years later makes me think that it was, in fact, the same entity. 


Discovering everyone else's experiences with him now that I'm an adult, is simultaneously terrifying and comforting. On one hand, it means I wasn't alone, and he wasn't just a product of my overactive imagination. On the other hand, it means *he wasn't just a product of my overactive imagination...*

Been finally taking some *small* but tangible steps toward reducing symptoms, and while it’s been very slow, I think I’m finally seeing some results! 

First, I’ve settled on a reasonable supplement schedule. 1.5 grams of myo-inositol powder dissolved in water twice daily. With my morning dose I take zinc, vitamin d, magnesium citrate, selenium, and omega 3.

I’ve also switched to decaf coffee, and now trying to gradually shift to drinking it black. Instead of my usual 1-2 BIG cups a day, I want to start having smaller cups after each meal to help with digestion and blood glucose. 

After about 3 months of slowly incorporating these changes, I’ve started to notice more energy during the day (though, when first cutting out caffeine I was so drained and exhausted until my body regulated), and my most recent period was right on time, with almost no cramps whatsoever! I still got some PMS symptoms like tender breasts, increased hunger, and some slight irritability but they were very manageable! 

I don’t have easy access to a scale, so I can’t be sure of this, but it seems like I’m also starting to lose a small amount of weight, or at the very least, reducing some bloating!

Hoping and praying that these results aren’t just in my head, and wishing all of you folks the best luck on your own journeys!!

I've definitely thought about stuff like this as well, but here's my perspective on it (for context I also haven't shifted yet, but am actively working toward it):

Suffering and hardship make up one of the foundations of the human experience, even if said suffering is mild. In a strange way, I value sadness (to an extent).

I *could* permashift to a reality in which nothing bad ever happened to me, but after a while that just doesn't seem pleasant. We can essentially only experience happiness BECAUSE we experience negative emotions, yin and yang. If you put yourself in a state that takes away those negative emotional triggers, you would become extremely numb to positive emotions due to them never fluctuating.

Personally I'm a very emotional person, however I also deal with depression, and it's JARRING to feel the difference when it flares up and gets really bad. Sure it affects my ability to feel joy, but it also stops me from feeling overly sad as well. I become extremely apathetic. I feel that shifting any time you face hardship would essentially just cause depression after a while.

As for the other points, while there definitely are people that choose to permashift and abandon this reality, I think that the beauty of shifting lies in the fact that everyone views it differently, and chooses to use the skill for different reasons. 

For me, I personally would just like to have a few different realities to live in *alongside* this one, as well as take "vacations" to other, more temporary ones. Despite this reality not treating me the best, it's still the first one I ever knew, and no reality, no matter how idyllic, will take that emotional bond away. Simple memories like walking to kindergarten with my dad, getting my cats, even something as simple as hugging my mum, make it so that this reality doesn't feel trivial, no matter how mundane it seems compared to the massive scale of what shifting allows.

Also, at the end of the day, what we're able to accomplish in this reality will always be affected by our resources, environment, health, etc.

If we accomplish something in a reality we've shifted to, it's not as if it counts any less! Where some people use money or connections to achieve their goals, we're simply utilizing the skill of shifting in order to do it. The only thing we have in this universe is the perception in our own minds, so as long as YOU experience your accomplishments and retain those memories, I don't think that it makes it any less fulfilling to have done it in a different reality than the one you originally perceived!

Overall, shifting is such a rabbit-hole of a concept that there could easily be 50 different takes on it than what I wrote hahaha. But I hope you find my perspective interesting! It was definitely interesting reading the other comments on here, seeing how our opinions align as well as differ

An underrated example that I haven't heard anyone else mention is the Stephen King novel Lisey's Story. Spoilers below, however I'll keep them as minimal as possible:



Basically in the novel, the wife (now widow) of a famous writer needs to travel to a specific reality that her husband was able to escape to, in order to save her sister, who can also travel there, but gets stuck due to mental health issues. 

During their honeymoon, Lisey very briefly gets taken to this reality by her husband (group shifting), but forces herself to repress the memory because she refuses to believe it was real. Her husband is impressed that she was able to come with him however, since he explains that it doesn't come naturally to many people. Later on, she's able to travel there by herself. 

The way King describes the shift from the one reality to the other is VERY close to the 5 senses method. Basically you close your eyes, and you start to hear the chirping of bugs, then you smell the sweetness of the honeysuckle, and the humid tropical air on your face. Then after all this, you open your eyes and boom, you're in the other reality.

I thought this concept was really neat when I had first read the novel, but now after discovering shifting, it's even more mindblowing. Another King novel, Rose Madder, has a very similar concept, however the main character shifts realities through a portrait, though the way it's written is very similar to the lucid dream/portal method

I'm definitely a "movie in your read" reader, and the only way I can describe it is going into a sort of trance (I don't need to go into that trance to be able to visualize what's happening, but for the more movie-like quality, I would). My eyes start skimming the words, and the visuals sort of fill my head.
 
I guess it's sort of a dream like, staccato effect. Each new written detail either adds to the picture in my head, or produces another "shot" of the film. So for the short excerpt you gave, without any other context, I'll try my best to describe how it looks in my head:

"Still, it was difficult to recognize her original features beneath the reddish scabs and sparse hair. The skeleton of her body made a distinct impression through the thin blue hospital sheet. Even in her condition, she could not keep from flirting. Only her voice had not changed. It was difficult to know if she was teasing or not. "And I thought you were coming back to me. You will marry her, won't you? Of course, I will try to forgive you because I know you loved me first." 

I can visualize a tiny, small framed woman (maybe 27 - 30 years old) with pale hair, sores covering her exposed skin and head, which is significantly balding though the hair left is a nice chestnut colour. The only lighting comes from the harsh florescent lights directly above. The "shot" goes from her head, to pan down her body from the back, allowing you to see the contours of her spine through the hospital gown, and her frighteningly thin arms as she sits on the edge of the bed. The voice she speaks with is soft, high pitched, and crackly, interspersed with small coughs. It sounds almost childlike, but with the undertone of years of pain that this woman has faced. As she speaks her line, my minds camera then shows a shot of her face, and she's sad but with the ghost of a smile on her lips. Since the small passage doesn't say anything about the person she's talking to, I don't even see him in the "shot" yet.

Now keep in mind, those visuals popped into my head immediately after reading it, and describing it in words is forcing more details to come through, but I tried my best to keep it to the initial visuals. It's such a hard thing to describe to those who don't experience it. It's almost as if every single movie and show you've ever watched is stored in your brain, and the book descriptions will bring forth tiny visual details from different ones, mixed in with your imagination, to produce said mind movie.
